summary: This RFC defines a new certificate request attribute, relatedCertRequest, and a new X.509 extension, RelatedCertificate. Together they give assurance that two certificates, for example one with a traditional key and one with a different algorithm, belong to the same entity. This supports protocols that authenticate with several certificates.

eli5.summary: If you carry two ID cards, someone should be able to tell both belong to you. This adds a way for one certificate to point to its partner.

questions: how to link two x.509 certificates
how does a ca verify a related certificate
subtitle: A certificate request attribute and an X.509 extension that prove two certificates belong to the same entity.

tldr.problem: A protocol that authenticates with two certificates, for example a traditional one and a post-quantum one, needs assurance that the same entity controls both private keys.
tldr.mechanism: The requester adds a relatedCertRequest attribute to its CSR, naming and signing over an existing certificate. The CA verifies it and issues a new certificate with a RelatedCertificate extension holding a hash of the old one.
tldr.outcome: A verifier can hash the other certificate it received and compare it with the extension, gaining assurance that both belong to one entity. The mechanism only expresses the relationship and does not enforce any security function itself.

today: RFC 9763 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata.

sections.title: Linking Two Certificates
sections.content:
The goal is to give assurance that two X.509 end-entity certificates are owned by the same entity, so a protocol can perform multiple authentications where each certificate corresponds to a distinct digital signature. The method tries to limit changes to the certificate format of RFC 5280 and to current PKI practice.

With non-composite hybrid public key mechanisms, the party relying on a certificate wants to know the private keys of both certificates are under the same entity's control. The RFC defines a certificate extension, RelatedCertificate, and a CSR attribute, relatedCertRequest, which lets a registration authority (RA) vouch for this to the certification authority (CA).
sections.eli5: When you have two ID cards, a friend can write on the new one, 'this goes with your other card.' This RFC makes that note official and checkable.

sections.title: The Overview: Cert A and Cert B
sections.content:
The design is illustrated by an entity with an existing certificate (Cert A) that requests a new one (Cert B), perhaps while migrating a PKI from traditional cryptography to post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

  • Where authentication is not negotiated, as in CMS and S/MIME, the signer may use Cert A's key, Cert B's key, or both, depending on which verifiers it anticipates.
  • Where authentication is negotiated in the protocol, as in TLS and IKEv2, either key may be used according to the verifier's preference, and peers may ask for both if the protocol allows.

The CSR attribute tells the CA how to locate Cert A and gives evidence the requester owns it. The CA verifies ownership before generating Cert B.
sections.eli5: You hold an old key and ask for a new one. You show the old key to prove you own it, and the new key comes with a note that it is a partner of the old one.

sections.title: The relatedCertRequest Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute carries a RequesterCertificate with four fields: certID, requestTime, locationInfo and signature.

  • certID is an IssuerAndSerialNumber that identifies the previously issued end-entity certificate the requester also owns.
  • requestTime is a BinaryTime value that ensures freshness, so the signed data can only be used at the time of the initial CSR.
  • locationInfo is a URI via HTTP(S) or a data URL. For the same CA organization it SHOULD be a URL to a file giving access to a CMS 'certs-only' message, with DER-encoded certificates. For a different CA organization it SHOULD be a data URL containing inline degenerate PKCS#7 with all certificates and CRLs needed to validate Cert A.
  • signature is a signature over the concatenation of the DER-encoded IssuerAndSerialNumber and BinaryTime, made with the private key of the certificate named in certID.

The attribute OID is id-aa-relatedCertRequest, defined as { id-aa 60 }.
sections.eli5: The request has four parts: which old card, what time you asked, where to find it, and your signature made with the old card to prove it is yours.

sections.title: How the CA Processes the Request
sections.content:
A CA that supports the attribute MUST retrieve the certificate named in the attribute and validate it using the path validation rules of RFC 5280, then compare its issuer and serial number with certID. It MUST check that requestTime is sufficiently fresh, which is defined by local policy, and MUST verify the signature using the public key of the related certificate.

The CA SHOULD then issue the new certificate with a RelatedCertificate extension referencing that certificate, and may apply local policy such as the remaining validity period. The RA MUST only allow a previously issued certificate in the attribute so the CA can perform the signature verification, and MAY send a CSR naming a certificate issued by a different CA.
sections.eli5: The card office finds your old card, checks the time and your signature, and only then prints the new card with the note on it.

sections.title: The RelatedCertificate Extension
sections.content:
The extension links the certificate that contains it (Cert B) to the one it references (Cert A). It holds a hashAlgorithm and a hashValue, which is the digest of the entire related certificate. If the related certificate's signature OID names a hash, such as ecdsa-with-SHA512, that hash SHOULD also be used here.

The extension SHOULD NOT be marked critical, since that would severely impact interoperability. In a chain it MUST only appear in the end-entity certificate. The issuing CA MUST only include a certificate listed in the CSR's relatedCertRequest attribute, MUST ensure the related certificate contains the key usage bits and extended key usage OIDs being asserted, and SHOULD determine the related certificate is valid at issuance.

A receiving endpoint that supports non-composite hybrid authentication should hash the other end-entity certificate and confirm the result matches the extension. What to do with the outcome is outside the RFC's scope and depends on each peer's policy.
sections.eli5: The note on the new card is a fingerprint of the old card. Anyone holding both can compare fingerprints to see that they match.

sections.title: Security and CA Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanisms only express that certificates are related. They do not by themselves effect any security function, and the recipient interprets them. The RFC says that for any hybrid approach there must be evidence the same entity controls all private keys at the time of use and at registration. It also warns that all hybrid implementations are vulnerable to a downgrade attack, in which a malicious peer does not express support for the stronger algorithm.

Fetching the related certificate from the URI carries risk, as a URL can point to malicious code, so retrieved data must be fully validated. Retrieval may be observed, so the data URL option is advisable if that matters. A public-facing CA may not validate certificates from other CA organizations, which may require pre-arrangement such as a contract and pre-configured trust anchors. The issuing CA should also match its certification policies to those of Cert A.
sections.eli5: The note proves the cards go together but does not decide anything alone. Be careful about where you fetch the old card from, and watch for tricksters who pretend they only have the weaker card.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered three OIDs, all referencing RFC 9763. In the "SMI Security for PKIX Certificate Extension" registry, decimal 36 is id-pe-relatedCert. In the "SMI Security for S/MIME Attributes" registry, decimal 60 is id-aa-relatedCertRequest. In the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry, decimal 115 is id-mod-related-cert-2023.

The registration procedure for the extension registry is Specification Required. Appendix A of the RFC gives the ASN.1 module that defines these types.
sections.eli5: The new names for the extension and the request note were written into the official list so everyone uses the same numbers.

items.text: Signature over certID and requestTime with the related certificate's private key.
